\section{Robustness of the share of the reachable range}
\label{app:share}
Table~\ref{tab:share} recomputes the shares of Table~\ref{tab:gapclosed} under the variants
of \S\ref{sec:gapclosed}. Each variant averages over items and runs at both ends and then
takes the share. The rows that start from $T{=}2$ or $T{=}4$ give the share of the range from
that $T$ to the floor or ceiling that $T{=}16$ closes. These ranges are smaller than the range
from $T{=}1$. The unpaired non-degenerate row averages each end over its own non-degenerate
items. The paired row keeps, per run, the items that are non-degenerate at both $T{=}1$ and
$T{=}16$. The next row keeps the items that are non-degenerate at every $T$ from 1 to 16.
The items column gives the mean number of items per run kept at both ends, and every
non-degenerate row keeps at least \NcrsNdMinItems\ items in each run. The paired and
every-$T$ rows use the mean SIM-o ceiling of the items they keep. Per-item WER floors were
not stored, so every row uses the floor over all \Nitems\ items, with two exceptions. The
floor-zero row sets the floor to zero, which lowers the intelligibility share, so it is the
cautious case. The F5-TTS row takes the WER and SIM-o of F5-TTS on the same items as floor
and ceiling. Only \NcrsFixedItems\ items are non-degenerate in every run at every $T$, too
few to report a fixed item set.

Part (b) gives the shares and the rate of degenerate outputs by parameter budget; budget D
has two seeds per shape. Longer training does not lower the rate at $T{=}1$: for the
\NtrendRuns\ runs of Table~\ref{tab:trend} it is \NcrsDegenThirtykTOne\% at 30k steps and
\NcrsDegenNinetykTOne\% at 90k. At 90k it is \NcrsDegenNinetykTTwo\% at $T{=}2$ and
\NcrsDegenNinetykTSixteen\% at $T{=}16$.
